board.text: Angles 48° and 66°. Which kind of triangle?

spec.note: What kind of triangle is it?

beats.say: A triangle has angles of 48 degrees and 66 degrees, and we have to name the triangle. But a triangle has 3 angles, and we only know 2.

ask.ifNot: Tear the 3 corners off a paper triangle and they fit along a straight line. A straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So before we name it, we need the third angle. What do the 3 angles of any triangle add up to?
180 degrees. So first add the 2 angles we know. 48 plus 60 is 108, and 6 more is 114.
Now take 114 away from 180. 180 minus 110 is 70, and 4 less is 66. The third angle is 66 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Look at the 66. It is there twice. So 2 of the angles are equal.

beats.say: Now look at all 3 angles together: 48, 66 and 66. What do you notice?
2 equal angles! And a triangle with 2 equal angles always has 2 equal sides as well.
A triangle with 2 equal sides is called isosceles. So this is an isosceles triangle.
Why not the other names? Equilateral needs 3 angles of 60. Right-angled needs a 90. Obtuse needs an angle bigger than 90. Ours has none of these.
So when only 2 angles are given, always find the third before you name the triangle. The name may be hiding in it.

board.text: Which set CANNOT be the angles of a triangle?

beats.say: Here are 4 sets of angles. 3 of them can be the angles of a triangle, and 1 cannot. We must catch the one that cannot.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles of every triangle add up to 180 degrees. Not more, not less. That is our test.

beats.say: We need a test. Every triangle obeys one rule about its 3 angles. What is it?
So we add each set and see whether it makes exactly 180. Start with A. 70 plus 60 is 130, and 40 more is 170.
170 is 10 short of 180. That looks suspicious. But let's test the others before we decide.
Set B. 75 plus 55 is 130, and 50 more is 180. That one can be a triangle.
Set C: 45 and 45 make 90, and 90 more makes 180. Set D: 30, 80 and 70 make 180 as well. Both pass.

choices: D, it has no right angle
ask.ifNot: Equal angles and right angles do not matter here. Only the total matters, and only set A misses 180.

beats.say: So which set cannot make a triangle?
Set A adds up to only 170. So 70, 60 and 40 degrees cannot be the angles of a triangle.
The rule to keep: 3 angles make a triangle only when they add up to exactly 180 degrees.

board.text: Triangle BED: base 6 cm, height 4 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Triangle B E D has a base of 6 centimetres and a height of 4 centimetres. We want its area, the space inside it.
Here is a neat trick for triangles. Draw a rectangle round the triangle, with the same base and the same height.

ask.ifNot: Cut the rectangle along the triangle's sides. The leftover pieces fit exactly on top of the triangle. So the triangle is half.

beats.say: How much of that rectangle does the triangle fill?
Half of it. So first we find the rectangle. 6 times 4 is 24.

ask.ifNot: 24 is the whole rectangle. The triangle is only half of it, so we still have to halve.

beats.say: Look, 24 is one of the choices. Is it our answer?
The triangle is half of the rectangle, and half of 24 is 12.
Now the unit. Area is measured in little squares, so it is 12 square centimetres, not just centimetres.
So for a triangle's area: base times height, then half. And always give it in square units.

board.text: Right triangle: base 19 cm, height 16 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: A right triangle has a base of 19 centimetres and a height of 16 centimetres. We want its area.

spec.note: Two of the triangles make a rectangle

beats.say: In a right triangle the base and the height meet at the square corner. Put 2 of these triangles together and they make a rectangle, 19 by 16.

ask.ifNot: 19 times 16 is the whole rectangle. Our triangle is one of its 2 equal halves, so we take half.

beats.say: So what is the area of one triangle?
First 19 times 16. Here is a quick way: 20 times 16 is 320. That is one 16 too many, so take 16 away. 304.
Now half of 304. Half of 300 is 150, and half of 4 is 2. So half of 304 is 152.

ask.ifNot: Look back at the question. The sides are measured in centimetres, so the little squares that fill the triangle are square centimetres.

beats.say: Now the unit, and here is the trap. The sides are in centimetres. So the area is in...
152 square centimetres. One of the choices has the right number but says square metres. Always read the unit as well as the number.
So: half of base times height, and match the unit to the question.

board.text: Which pair can be 2 angles of an isosceles triangle?

beats.say: Here are 4 pairs of angles. One pair can belong to an isosceles triangle. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Each pair shows only 2 of the triangle's 3 angles. The third angle is not shown, and it might match one of the pair.

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has 2 equal angles. But no pair here shows 2 equal angles. So where could the twin be hiding?
So for each pair we find the third angle. The 3 angles of a triangle always add up to 180 degrees.
Pair A. 63 plus 54 is 117. And 180 minus 117 is 63.
The third angle is 63, and the pair already has a 63. 2 equal angles! This triangle is isosceles.
Let's make sure about the others. Pair B: 75 and 45 make 120, so the third angle is 60. It matches nothing.
Pair C: the third angle is 51. That is close to 49, but close is not equal. Pair D: the third angle is 68. No match.
So the pair is 63 degrees and 54 degrees.
Whenever you see 2 angles of a triangle, find the third one. It often holds the surprise.

board.text: Two sides: 20 cm and 15 cm. Which CANNOT be the perimeter?

spec.note: The third side is not given

beats.say: 2 sides of a triangle are 20 centimetres and 15 centimetres. One of these 4 perimeters is impossible. Which?
Imagine 2 sticks, 20 and 15 centimetres long, joined at one end like a hinge. The third side has to close the gap between their free ends.

ask.ifNot: When the 2 sticks lie end to end in a straight line, the distance is both lengths together: 20 plus 15.

beats.say: Open the hinge wider and wider, until the 2 sticks lie in one straight line. How far apart are the free ends then?

board.text: Third side is shorter than 35 cm

beats.say: 35 centimetres. But a straight line is not a triangle! So the third side must be shorter than 35. That is the key idea.
The perimeter is all 3 sides: 35, plus the third side. The third side is less than 35, so the perimeter is less than 35 plus 35, which is 70.

ask.ifNot: The perimeter must be less than 70. Only one of the 4 is bigger than 70.

beats.say: So which of the 4 perimeters is impossible?
72. Check it: 72 minus 35 leaves 37 for the third side. But 37 is longer than both sticks put together, so they could never reach across.
The others are fine. Take 67: 67 minus 35 is 32, and 32 is shorter than 35.
So the perimeter cannot be 72 centimetres.
Remember the hinge. In any triangle, 2 sides together are always longer than the third. If not, they cannot meet.

board.text: Which pair can be 2 angles of an isosceles triangle?

beats.say: We need a pair of angles that can belong to an isosceles triangle. And there is a tempting last choice: none of these.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. So the third angle is 180 minus the 2 we know.

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has 2 equal angles. Each pair shows only 2 of the 3 angles, so the twin may be the third angle. How do we find a third angle?
Pair A has a decimal, but that is no problem. 64 plus 58.5 is 122.5. Then 180 minus 122.5 is 57.5.
57.5 is very close to 58.5. But close is not equal, and isosceles needs exactly equal. Pair A is out.
Pair B. 68 plus 44 is 112. And 180 minus 112 is 68.

ask.ifNot: The pair already has a 68, and the third angle is 68 too. 2 equal angles make the triangle isosceles.

beats.say: The third angle is 68. What does that tell us?
The angles are 68, 44 and 68. 2 of them are equal, so pair B works.
A quick look at C: 62.5 plus 54.5 is 117, so the third angle is 63. Close to 62.5 again, but not equal.
So the answer is 68 degrees and 44 degrees.
This question sets 2 traps: near misses, and none of these. Test every pair properly before you give up on them.

board.text: Which triangle has the same area as a square of side 9 cm?

spec.note: Which triangle has the same area as this square?

beats.say: A square has a side of 9 centimetres. We want the triangle that has the same area as this square.
First the square. Its area is side times side. 9 times 9 is 81.

board.text: Triangle area = half of base × height

beats.say: So we want a triangle with an area of 81. And the area of a triangle is half of its base times its height.

ask.ifNot: Half of the product is 81. So the whole product is 2 lots of 81, and that is 162.

beats.say: If half of base times height is 81, what must base times height be?
162. So now we just hunt for the base and height that multiply to 162. A: 12 times 4 is 48. Far too small.
B: 18 times 8 is 144. Close, but not 162. C: 12 times 14 is 168. Just over.
D: 27 times 6. 20 times 6 is 120, and 7 times 6 is 42. Together that is 162. Yes!
And half of 162 is 81, the same as the square. So the triangle has base 27 and height 6.
A tip: we doubled the target once, to 162. That saved us from halving 4 different products.

board.text: Sum of all the angles of a triangle = ?

spec.note: a + b + c = ?

beats.say: What do the 3 angles of a triangle add up to? Let's not only remember the answer. Let's see why it is true.
Imagine a paper triangle. Tear off its 3 corners.
Now put the 3 torn corners side by side, with their points together. Something lovely happens: they sit along a straight line.

ask.ifNot: Face forward, then turn until you face backward. You have turned along a straight line, and that is half of a full turn.

beats.say: How much turning is there along a straight line?
A half turn. And a full turn, all the way round, is 360 degrees.
Half of 360 is 180. So a straight line is 180 degrees.
So the 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. And this is true for every triangle, whatever its shape or size.
360 is tempting, but that is the full turn. It belongs to shapes with 4 sides, like a rectangle.
Keep this fact close. Almost every triangle question starts from it.

board.text: A triangle with all sides equal is called ...?

spec.note: All three sides are the same length

beats.say: This triangle has all 3 sides the same length. What is it called?
Triangles get names from their sides. There are 3 names to know, and each one tells you how many sides are equal.
When no sides are equal, the triangle is scalene. When exactly 2 sides are equal, it is isosceles.

ask.ifNot: Say them slowly. Equi-lateral begins like the word equal. Equi means equal, and lateral means side.

beats.say: Our triangle has all 3 sides equal. Say these names slowly. Which one sounds like the word equal?
Equilateral. Equi means equal, and lateral means side. Equal sides!
And right-angled? That name is about an angle, a square corner. It tells us nothing about the sides.
So a triangle with all sides equal is called equilateral.
A bonus fact: when all 3 sides are equal, all 3 angles are equal too.

board.text: A triangle with two equal sides is called ...?

spec.note: The two highlighted sides are the same length

beats.say: This triangle has 2 equal sides. We need its name.
Look at the picture. 2 sides are the same length, like the 2 legs of a ladder standing open. The third side is different.

ask.ifNot: Scalene is the name when all 3 sides are different. Keep it in mind, because we can cross it off.

beats.say: Let's clear away the names that do not fit. Which name is for a triangle with no equal sides at all?
Scalene means no equal sides, so that is out. Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal, and ours has only 2. Out as well.
Obtuse is a name about an angle, a wide one. It says nothing about the sides.
The name for exactly 2 equal sides is isosceles. It comes from old words that mean equal legs.
So a triangle with 2 equal sides is called isosceles.
Picture that open ladder with its 2 equal legs. That is your isosceles triangle.
2 angles of a triangle are 50 degrees and 60 degrees. We want the third angle.

ask.ifNot: Tear off a triangle's 3 corners and they fit along a straight line. A straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do the 3 angles of a triangle add up to?
180 degrees. So 50, plus 60, plus the hidden angle, makes 180.
First add what we know. 50 plus 60 is 110.

ask.ifNot: The third angle is what is left of the 180 after the 2 known angles take their share. So we take 110 away from 180.

beats.say: So 110 degrees are used up. How much is left for the third angle?
180 minus 110 is 70. The third angle is 70 degrees.
Check: 50 plus 60 plus 70 makes 180. And notice, a triangle does not need a 90 in it. That is a common mix-up.
So for a missing angle: add the 2 you know, then take the total away from 180.

board.text: A triangle with one angle of 90° is called ...?

spec.note: One angle is 90°

beats.say: A triangle has one angle of 90 degrees. What do we call it?
An angle of exactly 90 degrees is special. It is the corner of a book, or the corner of a door. A perfect square corner.

ask.ifNot: Acute means smaller than 90 degrees, and obtuse means bigger. An angle of exactly 90 is called a right angle.

beats.say: What do we call an angle of exactly 90 degrees?
A right angle. Acute angles are smaller than 90, sharp and pointy. Obtuse angles are bigger than 90, wide and open.
A triangle takes its name from its biggest angle. Here the biggest angle is the right angle.
So a triangle with one angle of 90 degrees is a right-angled triangle.
Why not equilateral? An equilateral triangle has 3 angles of 60 degrees each. It can never have a 90.
So: all angles sharp, acute. One square corner, right-angled. One wide angle, obtuse.

board.text: Sides: 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm. What kind of triangle?

spec.note: What kind of triangle is it?

beats.say: A triangle has sides of 5 centimetres, 5 centimetres and 8 centimetres. What kind of triangle is it?
Triangles are named by how many of their sides are equal. So let's compare the 3 lengths.

ask.ifNot: Look at the lengths: 5, 5 and 8. The 5 is there twice, and the 8 is on its own.

beats.say: How many of the sides are equal?
Exactly 2: the pair of 5s. The 8 is the odd one out.
Here are the 3 names. 3 equal sides: equilateral. 2 equal sides: isosceles. No equal sides: scalene.
One choice says these sides cannot make a triangle at all. Let's test. The 2 short sides together must be longer than the long side. 5 plus 5 is 10, and 10 is more than 8. So they do meet.
So it is an isosceles triangle.
To name a triangle by its sides, just count the equal ones.

spec.note: What kind of triangle is it?

beats.say: The angles of a triangle are 35 degrees, 55 degrees and 90 degrees. What kind of triangle is it?
This time we name the triangle by its angles. The trick is to look at the biggest angle.

ask.ifNot: Compare the 3 numbers. 90 is greater than 55, and 55 is greater than 35.

beats.say: Which is the biggest of the 3 angles?
90 degrees. Now the name depends on how the biggest angle compares with 90.

ask.ifNot: An angle of exactly 90 degrees is a square corner, and its name is a right angle.

beats.say: Our biggest angle is exactly 90. What is an angle of 90 degrees called?
A right angle. So this is a right-angled triangle.
And equilateral? That needs 3 equal angles. These 3 are all different.
So to name a triangle by its angles, find the biggest angle and compare it with 90.

board.text: All 3 sides are different. Its name, by its sides = ?

spec.note: All three sides have different lengths

beats.say: All 3 sides of a triangle have different lengths. By its sides, what is the triangle called?
There are 3 names for triangles by their sides. Each name counts the equal sides.
3 equal sides: equilateral. 2 equal sides: isosceles.

ask.ifNot: Isosceles needs 2 equal sides. Right-angled is a name about angles. The name for no equal sides is scalene.

beats.say: Our triangle has no equal sides at all. Which name is left?
Scalene. No 2 sides are the same.
Be careful with right-angled. It is a real triangle name, but it comes from the angles. This question asks for the name that comes from the sides.
So the triangle is a scalene triangle.
A way to remember: a scalene triangle looks a little lopsided, because nothing matches.

board.text: Isosceles: equal sides 9 cm each, third side 6 cm.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides of 9 centimetres each, and a third side of 6 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter is the walk all the way round the triangle. So we need the length of every side.

ask.ifNot: The question says 2 equal sides of 9 centimetres each. So the 9 comes twice, and the 6 comes once.

beats.say: What are the 3 sides?
9, 9 and 6. The 9 is there twice because it is the equal pair.
Now add them. 9 plus 9 is 18. And 18 plus 6 is 24.
So the perimeter is 24 centimetres.
2 slips to dodge. Adding only 9 and 6 leaves out a side. And multiplying 9 by 6 is not a walk round the triangle at all.
For a perimeter, list all the sides first, then add.

spec.note: Which name describes it best?

beats.say: A triangle has angles of 100 degrees, 40 degrees and 40 degrees. We want the name that describes it best.
The name has 2 parts. One part comes from the biggest angle. The other part comes from how many angles are equal.

ask.ifNot: 100 is more than 90. An angle that is bigger than a right angle is called obtuse.

beats.say: Start with the biggest angle, 100 degrees. A right angle is 90. So is the triangle acute-angled, right-angled or obtuse-angled?
Obtuse-angled, because 100 is more than 90. That is the first part of the name.
Now the second part. Look at the other 2 angles: 40 and 40. They are equal.

ask.ifNot: Scalene means no sides are equal, and equilateral means all 3. For exactly 2 equal sides the name is isosceles.

beats.say: 2 equal angles mean 2 equal sides. What is a triangle with 2 equal sides called?
Isosceles. Put the 2 parts together: it is an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.
So read the angles twice: once for the biggest one, and once for equal ones.

board.text: Which lengths CANNOT be the sides of a triangle?

beats.say: Here are 4 sets of lengths. 3 sets can be the sides of a triangle. One set cannot. Let's find it.
Think of 3 sticks. Lay the longest one flat. The 2 shorter ones rise up from its ends, and they must meet. They can only meet if together they are longer than the long stick.
So here is the test: add the 2 shorter lengths, and compare with the longest.
A: 3 plus 4 is 7, more than 5. Fine. B: 6 plus 6 is 12, more than 11. Fine, though it is a very flat triangle.
C: 7 plus 8 is 15, more than 14. Fine as well.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sticks together are exactly as long as the long one. They can only meet by lying flat on top of it. No triangle rises up.

beats.say: D: 4 plus 5 is 9, and the longest side is also 9. Can these 3 make a triangle?
They lie flat. Equal is not enough: the 2 short sides must be longer than the long side.

board.text: 4 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm cannot make a triangle

beats.say: So the set that cannot make a triangle is 4 centimetres, 5 centimetres and 9 centimetres.
The trap is the equal case. More than: yes. Only equal to: no.

board.text: Right-angled. One acute angle is twice the other.

spec.note: Right-angled. One acute angle is twice the other.

beats.say: In a right-angled triangle, one of the 2 acute angles is twice the other. We want the smallest angle of the triangle.
A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90 degrees. And all 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180.

ask.ifNot: Take the right angle away from the total. 180 minus 90 leaves 90 for the other 2 angles to share.

beats.say: So how much is left for the 2 acute angles together?
90 degrees, because 180 minus 90 is 90.
One acute angle is twice the other. So think in parts: the small angle is 1 part, and the big one is 2 parts.

ask.ifNot: The small angle is 1 part and the big angle is 2 parts. 1 plus 2 makes 3 parts.

beats.say: How many equal parts share the 90 degrees?
3 parts. So 1 part is 90 divided by 3, which is 30.
The acute angles are 30, and twice 30, which is 60. Check: 30 plus 60 plus 90 makes 180.
The question asks for the smallest angle. That is 30 degrees, not 60.
Parts make a twice as big question easy: count the parts, then share.

board.text: Isosceles: perimeter 40 cm, different side 12 cm.

spec.note: Perimeter = 40 cm. The two sides marked ? are equal.

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 40 centimetres. The side that is different is 12 centimetres. How long is each of the equal sides?
The perimeter is all 3 sides added together. One side is 12, and the other 2 are equal, like twins.

ask.ifNot: The 12 centimetre side is not one of the twins. Take it out of the perimeter first. What is left belongs to the twins.

beats.say: What should we do first?
40 minus 12 is 28. So the 2 equal sides together are 28 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: The 2 sides are equal, and they share 28 between them. So each one gets half of 28.

beats.say: 28 is for both twins together. How long is each one?
Half of 28 is 14. Each equal side is 14 centimetres.
Check: 14 plus 14 plus 12 makes 40. It works.
The trap is to halve 40 straight away. Always take off the odd side first, then share.

board.text: All 3 angles are equal. Sum of any 2 angles = ?

spec.note: All three angles are equal. Add any two of them.

beats.say: All 3 angles of a triangle are equal. We want the sum of any 2 of its angles.

ask.ifNot: The 3 corners of a triangle fit along a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do the 3 angles of a triangle add up to?
180 degrees. And here the 3 angles are equal, so they share 180 fairly.
180 shared among 3 is 60, because 3 times 60 is 180. So each angle is 60 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Read the question once more. It asks for the sum of any 2 of the angles, not for one angle.

beats.say: Is 60 our answer?
The question wants 2 of the angles added together. 60 plus 60 is 120.
So any 2 of the angles add up to 120 degrees.
Always read the last line of a question again before you answer. Here 60 was a step, not the finish.

board.text: Two sides: 7 cm and 10 cm. Third side: a whole number.

spec.note: The third side is a whole number of centimetres

beats.say: 2 sides of a triangle are 7 centimetres and 10 centimetres. The third side is a whole number. How long can it be at the very most?
Picture 2 sticks, 7 and 10 centimetres long, joined at a hinge. The third side stretches between their free ends.

ask.ifNot: End to end in a straight line, the 2 sticks reach 7 plus 10, which is 17 centimetres.

beats.say: Open the hinge until the sticks lie in one straight line. How far apart are the free ends now?

board.text: Third side is shorter than 17 cm

beats.say: 17. But at 17 the sticks lie flat, and a flat line is not a triangle. So the third side must be shorter than 17.

ask.ifNot: It must be less than 17, so 17 itself is not allowed. The next whole number down is 16.

beats.say: The third side is a whole number, less than 17. What is the greatest it can be?
16. Check: 7 plus 10 is 17, and 17 is more than 16, so the triangle closes.
And the 3 in the choices? That is 10 minus 7. It is near the shortest the third side could be, not the greatest.
So: add the 2 sides, then step just below. Equal is never enough.

board.text: Sticks: 3 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm, 10 cm. Pick 3 for a triangle.

beats.say: Jay has 4 sticks: 3, 5, 7 and 10 centimetres. He picks 3 sticks at a time to make a triangle. How many different triangles can he make?
There are 2 jobs here. First, list every way to pick 3 sticks. Then test each pick, because not every pick closes into a triangle.

ask.ifNot: Each time, exactly 1 stick stays behind. There are 4 sticks that could stay behind, so there are 4 ways.

beats.say: Picking 3 sticks out of 4 is the same as leaving 1 stick out. How many ways are there?
4 ways. Here they are, in order.
The test: the 2 shorter sticks together must be longer than the longest. First pick: 3 plus 5 is 8, and 8 is more than 7. A triangle!
Second pick: 3 plus 5 is 8 again, but now the long stick is 10. 8 is less than 10, so the sticks cannot reach.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sticks are exactly as long as the long one, so they can only lie flat along it. This is the trap in the question.

beats.say: Third pick: 3, 7 and 10. 3 plus 7 is exactly 10. Triangle, or not?
Not a triangle. Equal is not enough, so this pick is out too.
Last pick: 5 plus 7 is 12, more than 10. A triangle!
Count the picks that passed: 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10. That makes 2 triangles.
List in order, test every pick, and watch for the one where the short sticks only just equal the long one.

board.text: Isosceles. Top angle = 3 times each of the other two.

spec.note: Isosceles. Find the angle between the equal sides.

beats.say: In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the 2 equal sides is 3 times each of the other 2 angles. How big is that angle?
In an isosceles triangle, the 2 angles at the bottom are equal. Call each of them 1 part.
The angle between the equal sides, at the top, is 3 times as big. So it is 3 parts.

ask.ifNot: Do not forget that there are 2 bottom angles. 3 parts, plus 1 part, plus 1 more part, makes 5.

beats.say: How many equal parts are there in the whole triangle?
5 parts. This is where slips happen: counting only 1 bottom angle gives 4.
All the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. So 5 parts make 180, and 1 part is 180 divided by 5, which is 36.

ask.ifNot: 1 part is the size of each of the 2 equal angles at the bottom. The top angle is 3 parts.

beats.say: 36 degrees is 1 part. Which angle is that?
So each bottom angle is 36. The top angle is 3 parts, and 3 times 36 is 108.
So the angle between the equal sides is 108 degrees. Check: 108 plus 36 plus 36 makes 180.
Turn times as big into parts, count every part, then share out the 180.

spec.note: Together the three angles make 180°

beats.say: In a triangle, the second angle is 20 degrees more than the first. The third is 20 degrees more than the second. We want the largest angle.
Look at the bars. The second angle is the first plus 20. The third is the first plus 20 plus 20, so it is the first plus 40.
And all 3 angles together make 180 degrees.
Now imagine cutting off the extra bits, the 20 and the 40. What is left is 3 equal bars, each the size of the first angle.

ask.ifNot: Both extras come off, the 20 and the 40. That is 60 in all, and 180 minus 60 leaves 120.

beats.say: The extras are 60 altogether. So what do the 3 equal bars add up to?
120 for 3 equal bars. 120 divided by 3 is 40. So the first angle is 40 degrees.

choices: no, we want the largest angle
ask.ifNot: 40 is the first angle, and it is the smallest. The question asks for the largest, which is the third one.

beats.say: Is 40 our answer?
The second angle is 40 plus 20, which is 60. The third is 60 plus 20, which is 80.
So the largest angle is 80 degrees. Check: 40 plus 60 plus 80 makes 180.
When things grow by equal steps, cut off the extras first. Then share what is left.

board.text: Isosceles: perimeter 50 cm, one side 12 cm.

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 50 centimetres, and one of its sides is 12 centimetres. What can the other 2 sides be?
Isosceles means 2 sides are equal, like twins. But the question does not say whether the 12 is a twin, or the odd one out. So we must try both.
Case 1: the 12 is a twin. Then the sides are 12, 12 and one more. 12 plus 12 is 24, and 50 minus 24 is 26.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sides together make 24. That is less than 26, so they cannot meet above the long side.

beats.say: Sides of 12, 12 and 26. Can they make a triangle?
They cannot. 24 is less than 26, so the short sides never meet. Case 1 is the trap.
Case 2: the 12 is the odd one out. Then the twins share the rest. 50 minus 12 is 38, and half of 38 is 19.
Sides of 12, 19 and 19. Test them: 12 plus 19 is 31, which is more than 19. The triangle closes.

board.text: Other two sides: 19 cm and 19 cm

beats.say: So the other 2 sides are 19 centimetres and 19 centimetres.
And a pair like 14 and 24 does add up to the right perimeter. But then no 2 sides are equal, so the triangle is not isosceles.
2 checks every time: are 2 sides equal, and can the short sides reach across the long one?

board.text: Which statement about triangles is true?
A: A triangle can have two obtuse angles
B: An equilateral triangle can be right-angled
C: A scalene triangle can have two equal angles
D: A right-angled triangle can be isosceles

beats.say: 4 statements about triangles. Only 1 of them is true. Let's test them one at a time.
We test with 2 facts. The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. And equal angles always sit opposite equal sides.

ask.ifNot: Each obtuse angle is more than 90. So 2 of them make more than 90 plus 90, and that is already 180.

beats.say: Statement A. An obtuse angle is bigger than 90 degrees. What happens if a triangle has 2 of them?

target.text: A: A triangle can have two obtuse angles

beats.say: Too much! 90 plus 90 is already 180, and there is still a third angle to fit in. So A is not true.

target.text: B: An equilateral triangle can be right-angled

beats.say: Statement B. Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees. So it can never hold a 90. Not true.

target.text: C: A scalene triangle can have two equal angles

beats.say: Statement C. 2 equal angles always give 2 equal sides. But scalene means no equal sides at all. Not true.

choices: no, that is not a triangle
ask.ifNot: 90 plus 45 plus 45 is exactly 180, so it is a real triangle. It has a right angle, and it has 2 equal angles.

beats.say: Statement D. Can a triangle have a right angle and 2 equal angles as well? Try 90, 45 and 45.
It works. Fold a square of paper from corner to corner and you are holding exactly this triangle.

board.text: D is true: right-angled and isosceles

beats.say: So the true statement is D: a right-angled triangle can be isosceles.
To test whether a kind of triangle can exist, try to build one with real angles. If you can, it is true.

board.text: A 12 cm straw is cut into 3 whole-number pieces.

spec.note: Three whole-number pieces that can make a triangle

beats.say: Meera cuts a 12 centimetre straw into 3 pieces, each a whole number of centimetres, and makes a triangle. How many different triangles can she make?
The 3 pieces add up to 12. But they must also close into a triangle: the 2 shorter pieces together must be longer than the longest one.

ask.ifNot: If the longest piece is 6, the other 2 share the 6 that is left. They would be exactly as long as the long piece, and lie flat.

beats.say: Could the longest piece be 6 centimetres?
So the longest piece must be shorter than 6, which is half the straw. It can be 5 at most.
Longest piece 5. The other 2 share 7. They can be 2 and 5, or 3 and 4. Not 1 and 6, because then the 6 would be the longest.

ask.ifNot: Neither piece may be longer than 4, and together they must make 8. Only 4 and 4 does that.

beats.say: Longest piece 4. The other 2 share 8, and neither may be longer than 4. What must they be?
4 and 4. So the triangle is 4, 4, 4, an equilateral one.
Longest piece 3? Then 3 pieces of 3 or less make 9 at most. That cannot reach 12. So the list is complete.
Count them: 2, 5, 5 and 3, 4, 5 and 4, 4, 4. That makes 3 triangles.
The secret was to work in order, from the longest piece down. That way nothing is missed, and nothing is counted twice.

board.text: Two sides: 6 cm and 11 cm. Third side: a whole number.
How many different lengths can it have?

spec.note: The third side is a whole number of centimetres

beats.say: 2 sides of a triangle are 6 centimetres and 11 centimetres. The third side is a whole number. How many different lengths can it have?
The third side cannot be too long, and it cannot be too short. Let's find both ends. Think of 2 sticks joined by a hinge.
Open the hinge flat. The free ends are 6 plus 11 apart, which is 17. Flat is not a triangle, so the third side must be shorter than 17.

ask.ifNot: Folded shut, the short stick lies along the long one. The gap between the ends is the difference, 11 minus 6.

beats.say: Now close the hinge, folding the 6 back along the 11. How far apart are the free ends?
5. And folded flat is not a triangle either. So the third side must be longer than 5.
So the third side is a whole number, more than 5 and less than 17. It runs from 6 up to 16.

ask.ifNot: Point at each number once as you count: 6, 7, 8, and so on up to 16. The first number counts too.

beats.say: How many whole numbers are there from 6 to 16?
11. Here is a quick way. From 1 to 16 there are 16 numbers. Take away the first 5, which are not allowed. 16 minus 5 is 11.
So the third side can have 11 different lengths.
2 traps here. Counting 5 and 17, which lie flat. And working out 17 minus 5, which gives 12 and miscounts. Find both ends, leave them out, and count with care.

board.text: Isosceles. One angle is 4 times another.

beats.say: In an isosceles triangle, one angle is 4 times another. The triangle has no obtuse angle. We want its smallest angle.
Call the small angle 1 part. Then the big angle is 4 parts. Isosceles means 2 of the angles are equal. But which 2? And remember, the 3 angles make 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The equal pair could be the 2 small angles, or the 2 big angles. The question does not say, so both must be tried.

beats.say: What could the 3 angles be, in parts?
First case: parts 1, 1 and 4. That is 6 parts. 180 divided by 6 is 30.
So the angles are 30, 30, and 4 times 30, which is 120. But wait.

ask.ifNot: 120 is bigger than a right angle, so it is obtuse. And the question says the triangle has no obtuse angle.

beats.say: What is the matter with 120 degrees here?
It is obtuse, and the question does not allow that. So case 1 is out. This is the trap: 30 looks like an answer, but it is not.
Second case: parts 1, 4 and 4. That is 9 parts. 180 divided by 9 is 20.
The angles are 20, 80 and 80. None is obtuse, and 80 is 4 times 20. Everything fits.
So the smallest angle is 20 degrees.
When a question does not say which angles are equal, try every case. Then use the extra clue to choose.

board.text: Two isosceles triangles, each with an angle of 40°.
Different angle sets. Largest angles: difference = ?

beats.say: 2 triangles are both isosceles, and each has an angle of 40 degrees. But their angles are not the same. We want the difference between their largest angles.
How can 2 isosceles triangles both have a 40 and still be different? Because the 40 can sit in 2 different places.

choices: in the equal pair, or on its own
ask.ifNot: An isosceles triangle has 2 equal angles and 1 other angle. The 40 could be one of the equal pair, or it could be the other one.

beats.say: Where can the 40 degree angle be?
First triangle: 40 is one of the equal pair. The angles are 40, 40 and one more. 40 plus 40 is 80, and 180 minus 80 is 100.
Second triangle: 40 is on its own. The equal pair share what is left. 180 minus 40 is 140, and half of 140 is 70.
Here they are. One triangle is wide and flat. The other is tall and narrow.

ask.ifNot: Take the largest angle from each triangle. In the first it is 100. In the second it is 70.

beats.say: Which 2 angles must we compare?
100 and 70. Their difference is 100 minus 70, which is 30.
So the difference between the 2 largest angles is 30 degrees.
One angle of an isosceles triangle can mean 2 different triangles. Always ask: is it a twin, or the odd one out?

board.text: Isosceles: one side 5 cm, another side 11 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has one side of 5 centimetres and another side of 11 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
A triangle has 3 sides, and we are told only 2. But isosceles means 2 sides are equal. So the third side is a copy of one of the others.

ask.ifNot: The third side must equal one of the 2 sides we know. So it is either another 5 or another 11.

beats.say: What could the third side be?
Try 5 first. The sides would be 5, 5 and 11. Test them: 5 plus 5 is 10. Is 10 longer than 11? It is not.
The 2 short sides cannot reach across the 11. So 5, 5, 11 is not a triangle at all. This is the trap.
So the third side must be 11. The sides are 5, 11 and 11. Test: 5 plus 11 is 16, longer than 11. It closes.

ask.ifNot: A triangle has exactly 3 sides: 5, 11 and 11. Add those 3, no more and no fewer.

beats.say: Now the perimeter. Which sum gives it?
5 plus 11 is 16, and 16 plus 11 is 27. So the perimeter is 27 centimetres.
When a side is missing in an isosceles triangle, try both copies. Keep the one that can really close.

board.text: Sticks of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, plenty of each.
3 sticks make a triangle. How many different triangles?

beats.say: Aman has plenty of sticks of 3, 4 and 8 centimetres. He uses 3 sticks to make a triangle, and sticks may be the same length. How many different triangles?
The lengths may repeat, so we need an orderly list. First all 3 the same, then 2 the same, then all different.
All the same: 3, 3, 3 and 4, 4, 4 and 8, 8, 8. Equal sticks always close into a triangle. That is 3 so far.
Now 2 the same and 1 different. Take a pair, then add one of the other 2 lengths. That gives 6 picks.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sticks together make 6. That is less than 8, so they cannot reach across the long stick.

beats.say: Test 3, 3, 8. The 2 short sticks make 3 plus 3, which is 6. Does it close?
It does not. And 4, 4, 8 is sneaky: 4 plus 4 is exactly 8, so the sticks lie flat. Out as well.
The other 4 picks all close. 3 plus 3 is 6, more than 4. And when the pair is the longest length, it always closes.

ask.ifNot: 7 is less than 8. The 2 short sticks cannot meet across the 8.

beats.say: Last, all different: 3, 4 and 8. 3 plus 4 is 7. Is that a triangle?
No triangle there. So we have 3 with all sides equal, and 4 with 2 sides equal. 3 plus 4 is 7.
So Aman can make 7 different triangles.
Sort the picks into groups, test each one, and beware of the pick that only just lies flat.

board.text: Largest size the smallest angle can have = ?

beats.say: The 3 angles of a triangle are whole numbers of degrees, and all 3 are different. How big can the smallest angle be?
The 3 angles add up to 180. If one is small, the others are big. To push the smallest angle up, we want all 3 as close together as we can.

ask.ifNot: Equal angles share the 180 fairly. 180 divided by 3 is 60.

beats.say: If all 3 angles were exactly equal, what would each one be?
60 each. But the question says all 3 are different. So 60, 60, 60 is not allowed.

ask.ifNot: If the smallest is 60, the other 2 are both bigger than 60. Then the total is more than 3 times 60, which is more than 180.

beats.say: Can the smallest angle be 60 when the angles are all different?
So the smallest must be less than 60. Try 59. Then the other 2 share 180 minus 59, which is 121.
Can 2 different angles, both bigger than 59, make 121? Yes: 60 and 61.
58 works as well, with 60 and 62. But the question wants the largest size, and 59 beats 58.
So the smallest angle can be 59 degrees at most. The angles are 59, 60 and 61.
To make the smallest of 3 numbers as big as possible, squeeze the numbers close together. That gave us 59.

board.text: Which statement is true for EVERY triangle?
A: Its largest angle is more than 60°
B: It has at least two acute angles
C: Its two smallest angles add up to less than 90°
D: Exactly one of its angles is 60° or more

beats.say: 4 statements. Only 1 of them is true for every triangle there is. Which one?
True for every triangle is a strong claim. If we find even 1 triangle that breaks a statement, that statement is out. So let's hunt for rule breakers.
A good triangle to test with is the equilateral one. Its angles are 60, 60 and 60.

ask.ifNot: In the equilateral triangle the largest angle is 60. That is equal to 60, not more than 60. So it breaks statement A.

beats.say: Statement A says the largest angle is more than 60. Does the equilateral triangle obey?

target.text: A: Its largest angle is more than 60°
C: Its two smallest angles add up to less than 90°

beats.say: It breaks A. It breaks C too: its 2 smallest angles make 60 plus 60, which is 120. That is far more than 90.

target.text: D: Exactly one of its angles is 60° or more

beats.say: Now D: exactly one angle of 60 or more. Try a triangle with angles 40, 70 and 70. It has 2 angles above 60. D is broken.

choices: no, they would use up all 180°
ask.ifNot: 2 angles of 90 or more add up to at least 180. That leaves nothing for the third angle.

beats.say: Only B is left. But can it ever be broken? An acute angle is less than 90. Could a triangle have 2 angles that are 90 or more?
So at most 1 angle can be 90 or more. The other 2 must be acute, every single time.

board.text: B: at least two acute angles

beats.say: So the statement that is true for every triangle is B: it has at least 2 acute angles.
To knock out an always statement, find 1 rule breaker. To keep one, show why it can never be broken.

board.text: 5 equilateral triangles, side 4 cm, joined in a row.

spec.note: Five triangles in a row. Dashed lines are shared sides.

beats.say: 5 equilateral triangles, each with sides of 4 centimetres, are joined in a row, up, down, up, down, up. We want the perimeter of the whole shape.
Perimeter means the outside edge only. A side shared by 2 triangles is inside the shape, so it does not count.
Start by counting every side, as if the triangles were apart. 5 triangles with 3 sides each: 5 times 3 is 15 sides.

ask.ifNot: Look at the dashed lines in the picture. There is 1 join between each pair of neighbours, so 5 triangles have 4 joins.

beats.say: In a row of 5 triangles, how many joins are there between neighbours?
4 joins. Now the important part. At each join 2 sides are hidden, one from each triangle. So 4 joins hide 8 sides.
15 sides, take away the 8 hidden ones. That leaves 7 sides on the outside.

ask.ifNot: Only the 7 outside sides count. 15 counts every side, and 11 takes off each join only once instead of twice.

beats.say: Each outside side is 4 centimetres. So what is the perimeter?
7 times 4 is 28. The perimeter is 28 centimetres.
Check by walking round the picture: 3 sides along one long edge, 2 along the other, and 1 slanted side at each end. That is 7 sides.
When shapes are joined, every shared side disappears twice: once for each shape.

board.text: Sides: 3 consecutive whole numbers, like 5, 6, 7 cm.

spec.note: One example. Find the smallest triangle of this kind.

beats.say: The sides of a triangle are 3 consecutive whole numbers, such as 5, 6 and 7. What is the smallest perimeter such a triangle can have?
Consecutive means one after another, like 5, 6, 7. We want the smallest triangle of this kind, so we start from the smallest numbers.

ask.ifNot: A side cannot be 0 long. So the smallest set starts at 1, and it is 1, 2, 3.

beats.say: What is the smallest set of 3 consecutive whole numbers that could be lengths?
1, 2, 3. But do they close into a triangle? The 2 short sides together must be longer than the long side. 1 plus 2 is 3. Only equal!
Equal means the short sides lie flat along the long one. No triangle. So 1, 2, 3 is out, and its total of 6 is a trap.

choices: yes, so it is a triangle
ask.ifNot: 5 is more than 4. So the 2 short sides can rise up and meet above the long side.

beats.say: Next set: 2, 3, 4. 2 plus 3 is 5. Is that longer than 4?
5 is more than 4, so 2, 3, 4 is a real triangle.
Its perimeter is 2 plus 3 plus 4, which is 9 centimetres.
3, 4, 5 is a triangle too, with a perimeter of 12. But 9 is smaller.
Start small and test each set. The first one that closes is the winner, and here that gave 9.

board.text: Perimeter 30 cm. Each side is a whole number.
Greatest length of the longest side = ?

beats.say: A triangle has a perimeter of 30 centimetres, and each side is a whole number. How long can its longest side be?
We want one side as long as possible. But there is a limit. The other 2 sides together must still be longer than it, or they cannot meet.

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is 30. Take away the 15 centimetre side, and 15 is left for the other 2.

beats.say: Try a longest side of 15. How much is left for the other 2 sides together?
15 is left. So the other 2 sides together are exactly as long as the longest side. They lie flat. 15 does not work.
This is the trap. 15 is exactly half of the perimeter. The longest side has to be less than half.
Try 14. 30 minus 14 leaves 16 for the other 2 sides. And 16 is more than 14.
Can you think of 2 whole numbers that add up to 16, with neither longer than 14?
Here is one pair: 14 and 2. Sides of 14, 14 and 2 make a tall, thin triangle. 8 and 8 would work too.
So the longest side can be 14 centimetres at most.
And 28? That leaves only 2 for both of the other sides, far too little to reach across.
The longest side of a triangle is always less than half of the perimeter. Half of 30 is 15, so the best whole number is 14.

board.text: Right-angled. One angle is 4 times another.
All angles are whole numbers. Smallest angle = ?

beats.say: A triangle is right-angled. One of its angles is 4 times another, and all the angles are whole numbers. We want the smallest angle.
One angle is the right angle, 90 degrees. The other 2 share the rest: 180 minus 90 is 90.
Which 2 angles are linked by 4 times? Perhaps the right angle is 4 times a small angle. Let's test that idea first.

choices: no, it is not a whole number
ask.ifNot: The question says every angle is a whole number of degrees. 22.5 has a half in it, so it is not allowed.

beats.say: 90 divided by 4 is 22.5. Is that allowed?
Not allowed. That clue about whole numbers was there for a reason! So the 4 times link is between the 2 acute angles.
The small acute angle is 1 part, and the other is 4 parts. That is 5 parts, and together they make 90 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Only the 2 acute angles are being shared out. Together they make 90, not 180, and there are 5 parts.

beats.say: So how big is 1 part?
18 degrees. The other acute angle is 4 times 18, which is 72.
Check: 18 plus 72 plus 90 makes 180, and every angle is a whole number.
So the smallest angle is 18 degrees.
Use every clue in a question. Here the whole number clue told us which angles were linked.

board.text: Two sides: 9 cm and 4 cm. Third side: a whole number.
Perimeter is a multiple of 7. Third side = ?

spec.note: The perimeter is a multiple of 7

beats.say: 2 sides of a triangle are 9 centimetres and 4 centimetres. The third side is a whole number, and the perimeter is a multiple of 7. How long is the third side?
2 things must both be true. The sides must make a real triangle. And the perimeter must be in the 7 times table. Start with the triangle.

board.text: Third side: more than 5, less than 13

beats.say: The third side must be shorter than 9 plus 4, which is 13. And it must be longer than 9 minus 4, which is 5.
So the third side is 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12.
The perimeter is 13 plus the third side. So it runs from 13 plus 6, which is 19, up to 13 plus 12, which is 25.

ask.ifNot: Count in sevens: 7, 14, 21, 28. Only 21 lands between 19 and 25.

beats.say: Which multiple of 7 lies from 19 to 25?
21. So the perimeter is 21, and the third side is 21 minus 13, which is 8.
So the third side is 8 centimetres.
Watch the traps. A side of 1 gives a perimeter of 14, and a side of 15 gives 28. Both are multiples of 7, but neither closes into a triangle.
And a side of 7 is tempting. But it is the perimeter that must be a multiple of 7, not the side. The answer stays 8.

board.text: Triangle ABC is isosceles. Angle A = 50°.
Angle B is bigger than A and bigger than C. Angle C = ?

spec.note: Angle A (top) is 50°. Angle B (left) is the biggest. Angle C = ?

beats.say: Triangle A B C is isosceles. Angle A is 50 degrees. Angle B is bigger than angle A, and bigger than angle C. What is angle C?
Isosceles means 2 of the 3 angles are equal, like twins. The puzzle is: which 2?

choices: no, it equals neither of them
ask.ifNot: If B is bigger than A, it is not equal to A. If B is bigger than C, it is not equal to C. So B has no twin.

beats.say: Angle B is bigger than A, and bigger than C. Can B be one of the twins?
B is the odd one out. So the twins must be A and C.
Angle A is 50 degrees, so angle C is 50 degrees as well.
Let's check that B really is the biggest. 50 plus 50 is 100, and 180 minus 100 is 80. Angle B is 80, bigger than 50. It fits.
The trap is to make B and C the twins and share 130 between them, which gives 65. But twins are equal, and B has to be bigger than C.
So angle C is 50 degrees.
In an isosceles puzzle, first work out which 2 angles are the twins. The words of the question tell you.

board.text: Two angles add up to 110°. The bigger is 30° more.

spec.note: These two angles of the triangle add up to 110°

beats.say: 2 angles of a triangle add up to 110 degrees. The bigger one is 30 degrees more than the smaller one. What kind of triangle is it?
To name a triangle we need all 3 angles. So first let's find these 2, using the bars.
Cut the extra 30 off the bigger bar. Now the 2 bars are equal. Together they make 110 minus 30, which is 80.

ask.ifNot: The 2 equal bars share 80 between them. Half of 80 is 40.

beats.say: 2 equal bars make 80. How big is the smaller angle?
40 degrees. And the bigger angle is 40 plus 30, which is 70.
Do not stop here! 40 and 70 are different, so scalene looks tempting. But a triangle has a third angle.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180. The first 2 use 110 of it, so 180 minus 110 is left.

beats.say: The first 2 angles make 110. What is the third angle?
70 degrees. So the angles are 40, 70 and 70.
2 angles are equal, so 2 sides are equal. It is an isosceles triangle.
Never name a triangle from only 2 of its angles. Find the third one first.
A triangle has 3 angles. We are told 2 of them: 41 degrees and 40 degrees. Let's hunt for the third.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 40 plus 40 is 80. Then 1 more makes 81.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 81 away from 180.

beats.say: So 81 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 81 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 80: that leaves 100. Then take away 1 more: 99.
So the third angle is 99 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 41, 40 and 99. They make 180, just as they should. And notice: 99 degrees is a wide angle, an obtuse one. A triangle can have just 1 of those.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.

board.text: Angles in the ratio 3 : 1 : 1. Largest angle = ?

beats.say: The angles of this triangle are in the ratio 3 to 1 to 1. We want the largest angle.
A ratio is a way of sharing. Think of equal parts: the first angle gets 3 parts, the second gets 1 part, and the third gets 1 part.

ask.ifNot: Count every part of every angle. Add the 3 ratio numbers: 3, 1 and 1.

beats.say: How many equal parts are there altogether?
3 plus 1 plus 1 makes 5. So there are 5 equal parts in all.
Now the fact about every triangle: its 3 angles add up to 180 degrees. So these 5 parts share 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally means dividing. 180 degrees shared among 5 equal parts is 180 divided by 5.

beats.say: So how big is 1 part?
180 divided by 5 is 36. Multiply back to be sure: 5 times 36 is 180. So 1 part is 36 degrees.
Careful: 36 degrees is only 1 part, not the answer. The largest angle has the most parts, 3 of them. 3 times 36 is 108.
So the largest angle is 108 degrees.
Let's check with all 3 angles: 108, 36 and 36. Together they make 180. It works.
So with a ratio: add the parts, divide 180 by that to get 1 part, then multiply by the parts you need.

board.text: Triangle: base 12 cm, height 4 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a triangle. Its base is 12 centimetres and its height is 4 centimetres. We want its area, the space inside it.

spec.note: The triangle is half of the rectangle

beats.say: Picture a rectangle drawn round the triangle, with the same base and the same height. The triangle fills exactly half of that rectangle.

ask.ifNot: The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Adding the 2 numbers does not give the space inside.

beats.say: So let's find the rectangle first. Which sum gives the area of the whole rectangle?
12 times 4 is 48. That is the whole rectangle.

ask.ifNot: The triangle covers half of the rectangle, so its area is half of 48. We divide by 2.

beats.say: Here comes the step that is easy to forget. The triangle is only half of the rectangle. So what do we do with 48?
Half of 48 is 24.
So the area of the triangle is 24 square centimetres.
So for the area of a triangle: multiply the base by the height, then take half. Stopping at 48 is the classic slip.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 30 degrees and 37 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 30 plus 30 is 60. Then 7 more makes 67.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 67 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 67 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
Take 67 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 60: that leaves 120. Then take away 7 more: 113.
The hidden angle is 113 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 30, 37 and 113. They make 180, just as they should. And notice: 113 degrees is a wide angle, an obtuse one. A triangle can have just 1 of those.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.
This triangle is keeping a secret. We know 2 angles, 76 degrees and 58 degrees, and the third is hidden.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 76 plus 50 is 126. Then 8 more makes 134.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 134 away from 180.

beats.say: So 134 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 134 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 130: that leaves 50. Then take away 4 more: 46.
So the third angle is 46 degrees. There it is!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 76, 58 and 46. They make 180, just as they should.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.

board.text: Angles in the ratio 1 : 1 : 4. Largest angle = ?

beats.say: The angles of this triangle are in the ratio 1 to 1 to 4. We want the largest angle.
A ratio is a way of sharing. Think of equal parts: the first angle gets 1 part, the second gets 1 part, and the third gets 4 parts.

ask.ifNot: Count every part of every angle. Add the 3 ratio numbers: 1, 1 and 4.

beats.say: How many equal parts are there altogether?
1 plus 1 plus 4 makes 6. So there are 6 equal parts in all.
Now the fact about every triangle: its 3 angles add up to 180 degrees. So these 6 parts share 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally means dividing. 180 degrees shared among 6 equal parts is 180 divided by 6.

beats.say: So how big is 1 part?
180 divided by 6 is 30. Multiply back to be sure: 6 times 30 is 180. So 1 part is 30 degrees.
Careful: 30 degrees is only 1 part, not the answer. The largest angle has the most parts, 4 of them. 4 times 30 is 120.
So the largest angle is 120 degrees.
Let's check with all 3 angles: 30, 30 and 120. Together they make 180. It works.
So with a ratio: add the parts, divide 180 by that to get 1 part, then multiply by the parts you need.

board.text: Angles in the ratio 5 : 2 : 2. Largest angle = ?

beats.say: The angles of this triangle are in the ratio 5 to 2 to 2. We want the largest angle.
A ratio is a way of sharing. Think of equal parts: the first angle gets 5 parts, the second gets 2 parts, and the third gets 2 parts.

ask.ifNot: Count every part of every angle. Add the 3 ratio numbers: 5, 2 and 2.

beats.say: How many equal parts are there altogether?
