Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal. And when all the sides are equal, all the angles are equal too.

ask.ifNot: The 3 corners of a triangle fit along a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do the 3 angles of any triangle add up to?
180 degrees. So 3 equal angles share 180 between them.

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally means dividing. 180 shared among 3 angles is 180 divided by 3.

beats.say: How do we share 180 equally among 3 angles?
180 divided by 3 is 60. Multiply back to be sure: 3 times 60 is 180.
So each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees.
And this never changes. A tiny equilateral triangle and a huge one both have 3 angles of 60 degrees.

spec.note: An equilateral triangle. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: An equilateral triangle has a side of 7 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter is the walk all the way round. Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal, so every side is 7 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along all 3 sides, and each one is 7. So we add 7 three times.

beats.say: Which sum gives the walk all the way round?
7 plus 7 plus 7. That is 3 lots of 7, and 3 times 7 is 21.
So the perimeter is 21 centimetres.
Watch out for 7 times 7. That makes 49, and it has nothing to do with walking round a triangle.
And 4 times 7 would be right for a square, which has 4 sides. A triangle has only 3.
For any equilateral triangle, the perimeter is 3 times the side. Here that is 21.
2 angles of a triangle are 35 degrees and 65 degrees. Let's find the third.
Every triangle keeps one rule: its 3 angles add up to 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: We need to know how much of the 180 is used already. So we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: What do we do with the 2 angles we know?
35 plus 65. 30 and 60 make 90. 5 and 5 make 10. And 90 plus 10 is 100.

ask.ifNot: 100 is the 2 known angles together. The third angle is what is left of the 180.

beats.say: 100 is one of the choices. Is it the third angle?
180 minus 100 is 80. The third angle is 80 degrees.
Check: 35 plus 65 plus 80 makes 180. It works.
So: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.
A triangle has 3 angles. We are told 2 of them: 52 degrees and 59 degrees. Let's hunt for the third.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Add the tens first. 52 plus 50 is 102. Now the 9 that is left: that makes 111.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 111 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 111 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
Take 111 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 110: that leaves 70. Then take away 1 more: 69.
The hidden angle is 69 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 52, 59 and 69. They make 180, just as they should.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.

board.text: Two angles: 28° and 45°. What type of triangle?

spec.note: What type of triangle is it?

beats.say: 2 angles of a triangle are 28 degrees and 45 degrees. What type of triangle is it?
Both angles we can see are acute, small and sharp. It is tempting to say acute-angled straight away. But a triangle has 3 angles.
So find the third angle first. 28 plus 45: 28 plus 40 is 68, and 5 more is 73.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. So the third angle is 180 minus 73.

beats.say: The 2 known angles make 73. What is the third angle?
180 minus 73. Take away 70 to get 110, then 3 more to get 107.

ask.ifNot: 107 is bigger than 90. An angle bigger than a right angle is called obtuse.

beats.say: The third angle is 107 degrees. What kind of angle is that?
Obtuse. And one obtuse angle makes the whole triangle obtuse-angled.
It is not isosceles, because 28, 45 and 107 are all different. And 2 angles were enough to decide, because they give us the third.
Never judge a triangle by the 2 angles you can see. The third may be the big one.

board.text: Which lengths can be the sides of a triangle?

beats.say: Which of these sets of lengths can be the sides of a triangle?
Think of 3 sticks. They make a triangle only if the 2 shorter ones, put together, are longer than the longest. Otherwise they cannot meet.
A: 2 plus 5 is 7, and the longest side is 9. 7 is less than 9, so the short sides cannot reach each other.
So already we know that all of these cannot be the answer.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sides together are exactly as long as the long side. They can only lie flat along it. Equal is not enough.

beats.say: C: 1 plus 5 is 6, and the longest side is 6 as well. Is that a triangle?
Flat, so not a triangle.
B: 6 plus 8 is 14, and the longest side is 12. 14 is more than 12, so these sides can meet.
So the lengths that make a triangle are 6, 8 and 12 centimetres.
The test in one line: add the 2 shorter sides. More than the longest, a triangle. Equal or less, no triangle.

board.text: Which are the angles of an isosceles triangle?

beats.say: Which of these sets are the angles of an isosceles triangle?
An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides. And equal sides always come with equal angles. So we are looking for a set with a matching pair.

ask.ifNot: Look at set D: 30, 75 and 75. The 75 is there twice.

beats.say: Look along each set. Which set has an angle that appears twice?
Set D. The 75 appears twice.
A, B and C each have 3 different angles. Those triangles are scalene.
Let's make sure D is a real triangle. 75 plus 75 is 150, and 30 more makes 180. It is.
So the angles of an isosceles triangle are 30, 75 and 75 degrees.
For isosceles, hunt for the twins: 2 angles exactly the same.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 61 degrees and 26 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Add the tens first. 61 plus 20 is 81. Now the 6 that is left: that makes 87.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 87 away from 180.

beats.say: So 87 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 87 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 80: that leaves 100. Then take away 7 more: 93.
So the third angle is 93 degrees. There it is!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 61, 26 and 93. They make 180, just as they should. And notice: 93 degrees is a wide angle, an obtuse one. A triangle can have just 1 of those.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.

board.text: Right-angled triangle. One acute angle = 27°. Other = ?

spec.note: A right-angled triangle. Find the other acute angle.

beats.say: One acute angle of a right-angled triangle is 27 degrees. What is the other acute angle?
A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90 degrees. And the 3 angles of any triangle add up to 180.

ask.ifNot: Take the right angle out of the total. 180 minus 90 leaves 90 for the 2 acute angles.

beats.say: So what do the 2 acute angles add up to?
90. In a right-angled triangle the 2 acute angles always share 90. That is a handy shortcut.
One of them is 27. So the other is 90 minus 27. Take away 20 to get 70, then 7 more to get 63.
So the other acute angle is 63 degrees.
Check: 90 plus 27 plus 63 makes 180.
In a right-angled triangle, the 2 acute angles add up to 90. Just take the one you know away from 90.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 52 degrees and 73 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 52 plus 70 is 122. Then 3 more makes 125.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 125 away from 180.

beats.say: So 125 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 125 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 120: that leaves 60. Then take away 5 more: 55.
So the third angle is 55 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 52, 73 and 55. They make 180, just as they should.
That is the whole method. Add what you know, then find how far it is from 180.

board.text: Right-angled isosceles triangle. Each equal angle = ?

spec.note: Right-angled and isosceles: the two ? angles are equal

beats.say: A triangle is right-angled and isosceles at the same time. How big is each of its equal angles?
This triangle has 2 names. Right-angled tells us one angle is 90 degrees. Isosceles tells us 2 angles are equal.

ask.ifNot: 2 angles of 90 make 180 already. That would leave nothing for the third angle.

beats.say: Could the right angle be one of the equal pair?
So the right angle is the odd one, and the other 2 angles are the equal pair.
The 3 angles make 180. Take away the 90, and 90 is left for the equal pair.

ask.ifNot: Equal shares means halving. Half of 90 is 45.

beats.say: 2 equal angles share 90. How big is each one?
Half of 90 is 45. Each of the equal angles is 45 degrees.
Check: 90 plus 45 plus 45 makes 180. You can make this triangle by folding a square from corner to corner.
One name gave us the 90. The other name told us to halve what was left.

board.text: Which is NOT a type of triangle?

beats.say: 3 of these are real types of triangle. 1 can never exist. Which?

board.text: Acute: less than 90°. Obtuse: more than 90°.

beats.say: Each name has 2 parts, one about angles and one about sides. A type is real if we can find 3 angles that fit both parts. Let's try to build each one.
A: acute-angled isosceles. Try 70, 70 and 40. All less than 90, 2 are equal, and they make 180. Real.
B: obtuse-angled isosceles. Try 100, 40 and 40. One angle is above 90, and 2 are equal. Real.
D: acute-angled scalene. Try 50, 60 and 70. All different, and all less than 90. Real.

ask.ifNot: All 3 angles of an equilateral triangle are equal, and they share 180. So each one is 60.

beats.say: Now C: right-angled equilateral. How big is every angle of an equilateral triangle?
60, every one of them. But right-angled needs an angle of 90. An angle cannot be 60 and 90 at once!
And 3 angles of 90 would make 270, far more than 180.
So a right-angled equilateral triangle is not a type of triangle.
To test a type of triangle, try to build one. If the 2 parts of the name fight each other, it cannot exist.

board.text: Which are the angles of an obtuse-angled scalene triangle?

beats.say: Which set gives the angles of an obtuse-angled scalene triangle?
2 things must both be true. Obtuse-angled: one angle is more than 90. Scalene: all 3 sides are different, and so all 3 angles are different.

ask.ifNot: In A and B the biggest angle is exactly 90. That is a right angle, not an obtuse one. C has 120 and D has 150.

beats.say: First test: obtuse. Which sets have an angle bigger than 90?
C and D. In A and B the biggest angle is exactly 90, so those are right-angled triangles.

ask.ifNot: The 15 is there twice. 2 equal angles make a triangle isosceles, not scalene.

beats.say: Second test: scalene. Look at D: 150, 15 and 15. Are all 3 different?
D has twins, so it is isosceles. Out.
C: 40, 120 and 20. 120 is obtuse, and all 3 are different. They add up to 180, so it is a real triangle.
So the angles are 40, 120 and 20 degrees.
When a name has 2 parts, test one part at a time, and cross off as you go.

board.text: Exterior angle next to the third angle = ?

spec.note: Find the exterior angle next to the third angle

beats.say: 2 interior angles of a triangle are 55 degrees and 70 degrees. We want the exterior angle next to the third angle.
Interior angles are the ones inside the triangle. An exterior angle is made outside, when one side is stretched on past a corner.
First find the third inside angle. 55 plus 70 is 125, and 180 minus 125 is 55.
So the third interior angle is 55. Now stretch a side past that corner. The inside angle and the outside angle sit side by side on a straight line.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do 2 angles on a straight line add up to?
180. So the exterior angle is 180 minus 55. Take away 50 to get 130, then 5 more to get 125.
So the exterior angle is 125 degrees.
Did you spot it? 125 is also 55 plus 70, the other 2 inside angles added together. That always happens with an exterior angle.
The trap is 110. That is the outside angle next to the 70, which is a different corner. The one we want, next to the third angle, is 125.

board.text: Exterior angle = 130°. One opposite interior angle = 50°.

spec.note: The exterior angle at the bottom right corner is 130°

beats.say: An exterior angle of a triangle is 130 degrees. One of the opposite interior angles is 50 degrees. What is the other one?
An exterior angle sits outside the triangle, next to one corner. The 2 opposite interior angles are the inside angles at the other 2 corners.
Start with the inside angle right beside the exterior angle. Together they lie on a straight line, so they make 180. 180 minus 130 is 50.
So that inside angle is 50, and we are told another inside angle is 50 as well. And the 3 inside angles make 180.

ask.ifNot: The 2 inside angles we know are 50 and 50, which make 100. Take 100 away from 180.

beats.say: What is the last inside angle?
80 degrees. 50 plus 50 is 100, and 180 minus 100 is 80.
Now look at this. The 2 opposite angles, 50 and 80, add up to 130. That is exactly the exterior angle!
It is always true: an exterior angle equals the 2 opposite interior angles added together. So the quick way is 130 minus 50, which is 80.
Either way, the other angle is 80 degrees.

board.text: Isosceles triangle. Each base angle = 70°. Vertex angle = ?

beats.say: In an isosceles triangle each base angle is 70 degrees. We want the vertex angle.
An isosceles triangle has 2 equal base angles at the bottom, and 1 vertex angle at the top, between the equal sides.

ask.ifNot: An isosceles triangle has 2 base angles, and they are equal. So there are 2 angles of 70.

beats.say: Each base angle is 70. How many base angles are there?
2 of them. Together they make 70 plus 70, which is 140.
The 3 angles of a triangle make 180. So the vertex angle is whatever is left.
180 minus 140 is 40. The vertex angle is 40 degrees.
The trap is to take away only one 70 and say 110. Both base angles have to come off.
Check: 70 plus 70 plus 40 makes 180. So for the vertex angle, double the base angle and take it from 180.
This triangle is keeping a secret. We know 2 angles, 75 degrees and 74 degrees, and the third is hidden.
Every triangle, big or small, keeps one rule. Its 3 angles together make exactly 180 degrees.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 75 plus 70 is 145. Then 4 more makes 149.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 149 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 149 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
Take 149 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 140: that leaves 40. Then take away 9 more: 31.
The hidden angle is 31 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 75, 74 and 31. They make 180, just as they should.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.

board.text: Isosceles triangle. Vertex angle = 50°. Each base angle = ?

spec.note: The two base angles marked ? are equal

beats.say: The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is 50 degrees. How big is each base angle?
The vertex angle is at the top. The 2 base angles at the bottom are equal, like twins.

ask.ifNot: Take the vertex angle out of the 180. What is left belongs to the 2 base angles.

beats.say: The 3 angles of a triangle make 180. So what do the 2 base angles share?
130. That is both base angles together.

ask.ifNot: The 2 base angles are equal, and they share 130. So each one is half of 130.

beats.say: So how big is each base angle?
Half of 130. Half of 100 is 50, and half of 30 is 15. 50 plus 15 is 65.
So each base angle is 65 degrees.
Check: 50 plus 65 plus 65 makes 180.
When you know the vertex angle: take it from 180, then halve what is left.

board.text: The side opposite the right angle is called the ...?

spec.note: What is the highlighted side called?

beats.say: In a right-angled triangle, what do we call the side opposite the right angle?
A right-angled triangle has one square corner. 2 sides meet at that corner. The third side does not touch it: it lies across from the right angle.

ask.ifNot: In any triangle the longest side lies opposite the biggest angle. Here the biggest angle is the right angle.

beats.say: Look at the highlighted side. Compared with the other 2 sides, it is...
The longest. The biggest angle always faces the longest side, and the right angle is the biggest angle in this triangle.

board.text: Side opposite the right angle: hypotenuse

beats.say: This special longest side has a special name: the hypotenuse.

board.text: Base and height: meet at the right angle

beats.say: What about the other words? The base and the height are the 2 sides that meet at the right angle.
And a median is a line from a corner to the middle of the opposite side. It is not a side at all.
So the side opposite the right angle is called the hypotenuse.
Hypotenuse is a long word for a long side: the longest side of a right-angled triangle.

board.text: Axes of symmetry of a scalene triangle = ?

spec.note: A scalene triangle: all three sides are different

beats.say: How many axes of symmetry does a scalene triangle have?
An axis of symmetry is a fold line. Fold the shape along it, and the 2 halves match exactly.

spec.note: Equal sides fold onto each other

beats.say: In a triangle, a fold line goes through a corner. For the halves to match, the 2 sides that meet at that corner must land on each other. So they must be equal.

ask.ifNot: Scalene is the name for a triangle whose 3 sides are all different lengths.

beats.say: Now, what does scalene mean?
No sides are equal. So at every corner, a longer side would be folded onto a shorter one. The halves can never match.
No pair of equal sides means no fold line at all. A scalene triangle has 0 axes of symmetry.
Compare the others. An isosceles triangle has 1 fold line, through the corner between its equal sides. An equilateral triangle has 3.
So the number of fold lines tells you how many sides match. For a scalene triangle, that is 0.

board.text: Triangle with sides 8 cm, 11 cm, 15 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: A triangle has sides of 8, 11 and 15 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter is the walk all the way round the triangle, along every side.

ask.ifNot: Walking round means going along one side, then the next, then the last. The distances add up.

beats.say: So what do we do with the 3 lengths?
Add them. Start with 8 plus 11, which is 19.
Then 19 plus 15. 19 plus 10 is 29, and 5 more is 34.
So the perimeter is 34 centimetres.
Check by adding in another order. 15 plus 11 is 26, and 26 plus 8 is 34. The same answer.
Perimeter always means add. Multiplying the sides gives a huge number that means nothing here.

board.text: Perimeter 36 cm. Two sides: 12 cm and 9 cm. Third side = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = 36 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a triangle is 36 centimetres. 2 of its sides are 12 centimetres and 9 centimetres. How long is the third side?
The perimeter is all 3 sides added together. So 12, plus 9, plus the missing side, makes 36.

ask.ifNot: First find how much of the perimeter the 2 known sides use up. Add 12 and 9.

beats.say: What should we do first?
12 plus 9 is 21. The 2 known sides use up 21 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 21 is the 2 known sides together. The third side is what is still needed to reach 36.

beats.say: 21 is one of the choices. Is it the third side?
36 minus 21. Take away 20 to get 16, then 1 more to get 15.
So the third side is 15 centimetres.
Check: 12 plus 9 plus 15 makes 36. It works.
To find a missing side: add the sides you know, then take that from the perimeter.

board.text: Right-angled triangle with legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: A right-angled triangle has legs of 6 centimetres and 8 centimetres. We want its area.

spec.note: Two of the triangles make a rectangle

beats.say: The legs are the 2 sides that meet at the right angle. Put 2 of these triangles together and they make a rectangle, 6 by 8.

ask.ifNot: The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Adding gives a length, not the space inside.

beats.say: What is the area of that rectangle?
6 times 8 is 48. That is the whole rectangle.

ask.ifNot: 2 equal triangles fill the rectangle. So one triangle is half of 48.

beats.say: Our triangle is one of the 2 equal halves. So what is its area?
Half of 48 is 24. The area of the triangle is 24 square centimetres.
The 10 in the choices is the length of the third, slanted side of this triangle. That is a length, not an area.
For a right-angled triangle: multiply the 2 legs, then halve.

board.text: A median joins a vertex to the ____ of the opposite side.

beats.say: A median of a triangle joins a vertex to a special point of the opposite side. Which point?
A vertex is a corner. Every corner of a triangle has an opposite side: the one side that it does not touch.
A median is a line from a corner across to its opposite side. But it does not land just anywhere. Listen to the word: median sounds like middle.

ask.ifNot: Median and middle come from the same idea. A median lands exactly in the middle of the opposite side.

beats.say: So where on the opposite side does a median land?
Exactly in the middle. It cuts that side into 2 equal parts, like the 2 parts of 5 centimetres here.

board.text: Middle point of a side = midpoint

beats.say: The point in the middle of a side has its own name: the midpoint.
If the line went to an end point of the side, it would just run along a side of the triangle. That is no median.
So a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Median, middle, midpoint. The 3 words belong together.

board.text: How many medians does a triangle have?

beats.say: How many medians does a triangle have?
A median is a line from a corner of the triangle to the middle of the opposite side. Here is one.

ask.ifNot: Tri means 3. A triangle has 3 corners and 3 sides.

beats.say: How many corners does a triangle have?
3 corners. And each corner has exactly 1 opposite side, the side it does not touch.
So from each corner we can draw exactly 1 median. 3 corners, 1 median each: 3 medians.
So a triangle has 3 medians.
Why not 6? Because each corner gives only 1 median, not 2.
A lovely fact for later: all 3 medians cross at one single point, the balance point of the triangle.

board.text: Angles: 40°, 60°, 80°. Which side is the longest?

spec.note: Which side is the longest?

beats.say: A triangle has angles of 40, 60 and 80 degrees. Which of its sides is the longest?
Think of an angle as an open mouth. The wider the mouth opens, the longer the side it has to stretch across.

board.text: Biggest angle faces the longest side

beats.say: So the biggest angle faces the longest side, and the smallest angle faces the shortest side.

ask.ifNot: Compare the 3 numbers. 80 is more than 60, and 60 is more than 40.

beats.say: Which is the biggest angle here?
80 degrees. So the longest side is the one opposite the 80. Opposite means across from it: the side that angle does not touch.
So the longest side is the side opposite 80 degrees.
And the side opposite 40 is the shortest. The side opposite 60 is in between.
Could all the sides be equal? Only if all the angles were equal, and these are not.
Big angle, long side. Small angle, short side. Here the 80 wins.

board.text: Can a triangle have two right angles?

beats.say: Can a triangle have 2 right angles? Let's try to build one and see what happens.
A right angle is 90 degrees, a square corner.

ask.ifNot: Each right angle is 90. And 90 plus 90 is 180.

beats.say: 2 right angles together make how much?
180 degrees.
But the 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 altogether. The 2 right angles have used up all of it.

ask.ifNot: 180 minus 180 is 0. Nothing at all is left.

beats.say: So how much is left for the third angle?
0 degrees. An angle of 0 is no corner at all! The 2 sides would stand straight up, side by side, and never meet.
Making the triangle bigger, or its sides longer, changes nothing. The angles still have to add up to 180.
And a right-angled isosceles triangle has only 1 right angle. Its angles are 90, 45 and 45.
So the answer is no. 90 plus 90 is 180, and that leaves 0 for the third angle.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, perimeter 45 cm. Each side = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = 45 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 45 centimetres. How long is each side?
Equilateral means 3 equal sides. Together the 3 sides make the perimeter, 45.

ask.ifNot: The 45 is shared equally among 3 sides. Sharing equally means dividing, and there are 3 sides.

beats.say: How do we find 1 side?
45 divided by 3. Split 45 into 30 and 15. 30 divided by 3 is 10, and 15 divided by 3 is 5. 10 plus 5 is 15.
So each side is 15 centimetres.
Check: 15 plus 15 plus 15 makes 45.
2 slips to dodge. Multiplying by 3 makes one side longer than the whole perimeter. And dividing by 2 forgets that a triangle has 3 sides.
Perimeter of an equilateral triangle, divided by 3, gives the side.

board.text: Right-angled triangle: base 12 cm, area 42 cm². Height = ?

spec.note: Area = 42 cm²

beats.say: A right-angled triangle has a base of 12 centimetres and an area of 42 square centimetres. What is its height?
We know how to go forwards: the area is half of base times height. This time we go backwards, from the area to the height.

ask.ifNot: Twice means 2 lots. 42 plus 42 is 84.

beats.say: The triangle is half of a rectangle with the same base and height. So the rectangle's area is twice 42. What is twice 42?
84. So the base times the height is 84.

ask.ifNot: To undo times 12, we divide by 12. So the height is 84 divided by 12.

beats.say: 12 times what makes 84?
84 divided by 12 is 7, because 12 times 7 is 84.
So the height is 7 centimetres.
Check forwards: 12 times 7 is 84, and half of 84 is 42. That matches the area.
The trap is 42 divided by 12, which gives 3.5. That forgets the half. Double the area first, then divide by the base. That gives 7.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 32 degrees and 73 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 32 plus 70 is 102. Then 3 more makes 105.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 105 away from 180.

beats.say: So 105 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 105 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 100: that leaves 80. Then take away 5 more: 75.
So the third angle is 75 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 32, 73 and 75. They make 180, just as they should.
That is the whole method. Add what you know, then find how far it is from 180.
